The spheroid in spheroidal coordinates ​

See also

Theory: Spheroidal coordinates · Ellipsoidal coordinates · Curvilinear differential calculus · Spheroidal harmonics and their re-expansion · Submanifolds

Manual: Coordinate systems (symbolic) · Charts and coordinate conversions · Spheroidal harmonics · Submanifolds

Tutorials: Ellipsoidal coordinates · Changing the focal distance of spheroidal harmonics · Surfaces: fundamental forms and curvature

The spheroidal coordinates are the system in which a spheroidal inclusion is a coordinate surface. This tutorial builds the prolate system step by step and recovers, with TensND, the results that a problem set on a spheroid needs: the Lamé coefficients and the unit vectors, the volume and the surface of a spheroid, the gradient, the divergence and the Laplacian, then the spheroid seen as a surface, with its curvatures and its surface operators. They are the formulas of the appendix on spheroidal coordinates of Barthélémy and Bignonnet (2020), derived on Spheroidal coordinates. The oblate system follows by a substitution, checked at the end.

julia
using TensND
using LinearAlgebra
using SymPyPythonCall
using Plots

The chart ​

With the semi-focal distance,    and  , the point of coordinates is

coorsys_spheroidal returns the system. Its position vector is written with the two auxiliary symbols   and  , which keep the expressions short:

julia
Spheroidal = coorsys_spheroidal()
ϕ, p, q = get_coords(Spheroidal)
c = symbols("c", positive = true)
position_vector(Spheroidal)

The same map between symbols, without auxiliary symbols, is the chart:

julia
chart = ProlateSpheroidalChart(c)
x₁, x₂, x₃ = coords_to_cartesian(chart, (ϕ, p, q))

The surface   is a spheroid of semi-axes   along and across:

julia
simplify((x₁^2 + x₂^2) / (c^2 * (q^2 - 1)) + x₃^2 / (c^2 * q^2))

The position vector is also a combination of two spheroidal harmonics of degree one,

with the Legendre functions of legendre_P on   and of radial_P beyond. Both return the degrees to , the degree at the index  :

julia
P₁¹p = legendre_P(1, 1, p)[2]
P₁¹q = radial_P(chart, 1, 1, q)[2]
P₁¹p, P₁¹q
(-sqrt((1 - p)*(p + 1)), sqrt(q^2 - 1))
julia
simplify(x₁ + c * P₁¹p * P₁¹q * cos(ϕ)), simplify(x₃ - c * legendre_P(1, 0, p)[2] * radial_P(chart, 1, 0, q)[2])
(0, 0)

Lamé coefficients and unit vectors ​

The natural vectors are the derivatives of the position vector with respect to the coordinates; their norms are the Lamé coefficients

julia
χᵩ, χₚ, χ_q = lame_coefficients(Spheroidal)
(c*sqrt(1 - p^2)*sqrt(q^2 - 1), c*sqrt(-p^2 + q^2)/sqrt(1 - p^2), c*sqrt(-p^2 + q^2)/sqrt(q^2 - 1))

The unit vectors are the columns of the normalized basis, in Cartesian components:

julia
ℬ = normalized_basis(Spheroidal)
𝐞ᵠ, 𝐞ᵖ, 𝐞q = unitvec(Spheroidal)
Matrix(ℬ)

They are orthonormal, and each natural vector is its unit vector times its Lamé coefficient. The check differentiates the chart directly:

julia
E = Matrix(ℬ)
J = [diff(xᵢ, ξ) for xᵢ in (x₁, x₂, x₃), ξ in (ϕ, p, q)]
simplify.(transpose(E) * E), simplify.(J - E * Diagonal([χᵩ, χₚ, χ_q]))
(Sym{PythonCall.Py}[1 0 0; 0 1 0; 0 0 1], Sym{PythonCall.Py}[0 0 0; 0 0 0; 0 0 0])

Volume and surface of a spheroid ​

The volume element is the product of the three Lamé coefficients and the surface element of a spheroid   the product of the two tangent ones:

julia
dΩ = simplify(χᵩ * χₚ * χ_q)
dS = simplify(χᵩ * χₚ)
dΩ, dS
(c^3*(-p^2 + q^2), c^2*sqrt(-p^2 + q^2)*sqrt(q^2 - 1))

Integrating over   and   , and for the volume over the radial coordinate from the focal segment   to the spheroid:

julia
t = symbols("t", positive = true)
V = factor(integrate(integrate(integrate(dΩ(q => t), (ϕ, 0, 2PI)), (p, -1, 1)), (t, 1, q)))

julia
S = simplify(integrate(integrate(dS, (ϕ, 0, 2PI)), (p, -1, 1)))

which are       and     . In terms of the equatorial radius   and of the aspect ratio   , the volume is   :

julia
b, ω = symbols("b ω", positive = true)
simplify(V(c => b / sqrt(q^2 - 1)) / (Sym(4) / 3 * PI * b^3) - q / sqrt(q^2 - 1))

The specific surface   measures how much interface a given volume of inclusions carries. Compared with that of the sphere of the same volume, with   , it only depends on the aspect ratio. The oblate branch   uses the oblate formulas obtained at the end of this page.

julia
σ_prolate(ω) = (q = ω / sqrt(ω^2 - 1); ω^(-2 / 3) / 2 * (1 + q^2 / sqrt(q^2 - 1) * asin(1 / q)))
σ_oblate(ω) = (τ = ω / sqrt(1 - ω^2); ω^(-2 / 3) / 2 * (1 + τ^2 / sqrt(τ^2 + 1) * asinh(1 / τ)))
ωs_oblate = 10 .^ range(-2, -0.01; length = 100)
ωs_prolate = 10 .^ range(0.01, 2; length = 100)
plot(
    ωs_oblate, σ_oblate.(ωs_oblate); label = "oblate", xscale = :log10, lw = 2,
    xlabel = "aspect ratio ω", ylabel = "specific surface / that of the sphere of the same volume",
    legend = :top, size = (700, 420), guidefontsize = 9,
)
plot!(ωs_prolate, σ_prolate.(ωs_prolate); label = "prolate", lw = 2)
scatter!([1.0], [1.0]; label = "sphere", color = :black)

A needle ( ) and a disk ( ) both expose much more surface than the sphere of the same volume.

Gradient, divergence and Laplacian ​

The operators apply to any field of the coordinates. For a scalar field , the physical components of the gradient are the partial derivatives divided by the Lamé coefficients:

julia
f = SymFunction("f", real = true)(ϕ, p, q)
simplify.(components(grad(f, Spheroidal), ℬ))

The Laplacian is compared with its expression in an orthogonal system,

julia
Δf = (diff((1 - p^2) * diff(f, p), p) + diff((q^2 - 1) * diff(f, q), q)) / (c^2 * (q^2 - p^2)) +
    diff(f, ϕ, 2) / (c^2 * (1 - p^2) * (q^2 - 1))
simplify(laplacian(f, Spheroidal) - Δf)

For a vector field of physical components ,

julia
vᵩ, vₚ, v_q = (SymFunction("v$i", real = true)(ϕ, p, q) for i in ("ϕ", "p", "q"))
𝐯 = vᵩ * 𝐞ᵠ + vₚ * 𝐞ᵖ + v_q * 𝐞q
D = q^2 - p^2
divv = diff(vᵩ, ϕ) / (c * sqrt(1 - p^2) * sqrt(q^2 - 1)) +
    (diff(sqrt(1 - p^2) * sqrt(D) * vₚ, p) + diff(sqrt(q^2 - 1) * sqrt(D) * v_q, q)) / (c * D)
simplify(divergence(𝐯, Spheroidal) - divv)

The Laplace equation separates in these coordinates, and its solutions are products of Legendre functions of and of . The exterior harmonic of degree one,   with     , is the potential outside a spheroid placed in a uniform field along its axis:

julia
simplify(laplacian(p * (q * acoth(q) - 1), Spheroidal))

The spheroid as a coordinate surface ​

On the spheroid  , the unit normal is and are coordinates of the surface. The gradient of the normal field, read in the normalized basis, is minus the curvature tensor of the surface (Weingarten): its diagonal holds the principal curvatures with their sign changed.

julia
𝐧 = 𝐞q
∇𝐧 = simplify.(components(grad(𝐧, Spheroidal), ℬ))

The principal curvatures along and are therefore

negative because the normal points outward:

julia
κᵩ, κₚ = -∇𝐧[1, 1], -∇𝐧[2, 2]
(-q/(c*sqrt(-p^2 + q^2)*sqrt(q^2 - 1)), -q*sqrt(q^2 - 1)/(c*(-p^2 + q^2)^(3/2)))

At the equator they are the inverse of the equatorial radius and the curvature of the meridian ellipse at the end of its minor axis, with    and  :

julia
simplify(κᵩ(p => 0) + 1 / (c * sqrt(q^2 - 1))), simplify(κₚ(p => 0) + c * sqrt(q^2 - 1) / (c * q)^2)
(0, 0)

The divergence of the normal is minus their sum, twice the mean curvature up to the sign:

julia
simplify(divergence(𝐧, Spheroidal)), simplify(divergence(𝐧, Spheroidal) + κᵩ + κₚ)
(q*(-p^2 + 2*q^2 - 1)/(c*(-p^2 + q^2)^(3/2)*sqrt(q^2 - 1)), 0)

Surface operators ​

A field defined on the spheroid depends on only. Its surface gradient is its gradient, which has no component along the normal:

julia
g = SymFunction("g", real = true)(ϕ, p)
∇g = grad(g, Spheroidal)
simplify.(components(∇g, ℬ))

The surface divergence of a field removes from the divergence the stretching along the normal,       :

julia
div_S(𝐰) = divergence(𝐰, Spheroidal) - 𝐧 ⋅ (grad(𝐰, Spheroidal) ⋅ 𝐧)
div_S (generic function with 1 method)

For a tangent field      it is

julia
wᵩ, wₚ = (SymFunction("w$i", real = true)(ϕ, p) for i in ("ϕ", "p"))
𝐰 = wᵩ * 𝐞ᵠ + wₚ * 𝐞ᵖ
simplify(div_S(𝐰) - (diff(χₚ * wᵩ, ϕ) + diff(χᵩ * wₚ, p)) / (χᵩ * χₚ))

The surface Laplacian is the surface divergence of the surface gradient. It is the operator that the conditions on an imperfect interface involve:

julia
Δ_Sg = (diff(g, ϕ, 2) / ((1 - p^2) * (q^2 - 1)) + diff((1 - p^2) / sqrt(D) * diff(g, p), p) / sqrt(D)) / c^2
simplify(div_S(∇g) - Δ_Sg)

The same spheroid as a submanifold ​

A Submanifold is built from the position vector of a surface alone, without the system around it. The spheroid  ,   is parameterized by the colatitude-like angle such that  , and by ; in this order the normal points outward.

julia
ϑ = symbols("ϑ", real = true)
q₀ = Sym(2)
Spheroid = Submanifold(
    Tens([sqrt(q₀^2 - 1) * sin(ϑ) * cos(ϕ), sqrt(q₀^2 - 1) * sin(ϑ) * sin(ϕ), q₀ * cos(ϑ)]),
    (ϑ, ϕ); rules = Dict(abs(sin(ϑ)) => sin(ϑ)),
)
simplify.(canonical_components(normal(Spheroid)))

Its first and second fundamental forms:

julia
𝐚 = simplify.(get_array(submetric(Spheroid))[1:2, 1:2])
𝐛 = simplify.(get_array(curvature(Spheroid))[1:2, 1:2])
𝐚, 𝐛
(Sym{PythonCall.Py}[sin(ϑ)^2 + 3 0; 0 3*sin(ϑ)^2], Sym{PythonCall.Py}[-2*sqrt(3)/sqrt(sin(ϑ)^2 + 3) 0; 0 -2*sqrt(3)*sin(ϑ)^2/sqrt(sin(ϑ)^2 + 3)])

The eigenvalues of are the principal curvatures, here along then . They are those found above, at  ,   and  :

julia
at(e) = e(c => 1, q => q₀, p => cos(ϑ))
simplify.(diag(inv(𝐚) * 𝐛) - [at(κₚ), at(κᵩ)])

The operators of a submanifold are the surface operators. The Laplacian of a field is compared with above, in which    :

julia
h = SymFunction("h", real = true)(ϑ, ϕ)
D₀ = q₀^2 - cos(ϑ)^2
Δ_Sh = diff(h, ϕ, 2) / (sin(ϑ)^2 * (q₀^2 - 1)) + diff(sin(ϑ) / sqrt(D₀) * diff(h, ϑ), ϑ) / (sqrt(D₀) * sin(ϑ))
simplify(laplacian(h, Spheroid) - Δ_Sh)

The oblate system ​

The oblate system revolves the same confocal conics about the other axis. It is the prolate one in which is replaced by   and by  :

julia
Oblate = coorsys_spheroidal_oblate()
τ = get_coords(Oblate)[3]
lame_coefficients(Oblate)
(c*sqrt(1 - p^2)*sqrt(τ^2 + 1), c*sqrt(p^2 + τ^2)/sqrt(1 - p^2), c*sqrt(p^2 + τ^2)/sqrt(τ^2 + 1))

The substitution is checked on the squares of the Lamé coefficients, which involve no choice of branch. Since   , the line element   becomes  , so that is the image of :

julia
to_oblate(e) = e(c => -IM * c, q => IM * τ)
simplify.(to_oblate.((χᵩ^2, χₚ^2, -χ_q^2)) .- lame_coefficients(Oblate) .^ 2)
(0, 0, 0)

and it turns the volume of the prolate spheroid into that of the oblate one,     :

julia
factor(simplify(to_oblate(V)))

The operators are obtained in the same way, or directly from the oblate system. Its Laplacian has   replaced by   and   by  :

julia
fₒ = SymFunction("f", real = true)(ϕ, p, τ)
Δfₒ = (diff((1 - p^2) * diff(fₒ, p), p) + diff((τ^2 + 1) * diff(fₒ, τ), τ)) / (c^2 * (τ^2 + p^2)) +
    diff(fₒ, ϕ, 2) / (c^2 * (1 - p^2) * (τ^2 + 1))
simplify(laplacian(fₒ, Oblate) - Δfₒ)

The surface of the oblate spheroid follows from its own surface element:

julia
dSₒ = simplify(prod(lame_coefficients(Oblate)[1:2]))
Sₒ = simplify(integrate(integrate(dSₒ, (ϕ, 0, 2PI)), (p, -1, 1)))

that is     , the expression used for the specific surface plotted above.

The harmonics of the two systems, and the change from a system to another of a different focal distance, are the subject of Changing the focal distance of spheroidal harmonics.
